## Question

_Who does the work, carries the risk, or has no recourse?_

A generative AI system looks automatic. Behind it, people collect and label data, rate answers, moderate content, maintain hardware, and write the texts and images that the system learned from. This lens follows the lifecycle of a model and asks who works at each stage, who carries the risk, and who can object.

## Core concepts

### 1. The lifecycle has six stages

The course uses six stages: **design → data → training → deployment → evaluation → governance**. This framework builds on Rachel Huber and Moritz Mähr's _Decoding Inequality_ course, published in 2024 and updated in 2025 [@huber2024]. Its original labels are architecture selection, data collection, training, application, evaluation and monitoring, and governance and regulation. The course uses shorter labels. The order is a convention of the course. Evaluation happens before and after deployment, and governance applies at every stage. Each stage involves different people and different risks. Suresh and Guttag show that harm can enter at many points of the machine learning lifecycle, from the collection of data to the deployment of a model [-@suresh2021]. Weidinger et al. sort the risks of language models into six areas, from discrimination and misinformation to environmental and socioeconomic harms [-@weidinger2022].

![The six-stage framework builds on Huber and Mähr (2024; updated 2025). Original diagram: Laura Wagner and Moritz Mähr (2026), CC BY 4.0. Suresh and Guttag (2021) research lifecycle harms; they did not author these six stages.](../../assets/cases/03-lifecycle.svg){fig-alt="Six stages in a cycle: design, data, training, deployment, evaluation, governance. Evaluation repeats and governance applies at every stage. Framework: Huber and Mähr, 2024, updated 2025. Diagram: Wagner and Mähr, 2026."}

### 2. Labor is hidden behind "automation"

- **Ghost work.** Gray and Suri describe task-based, on-demand work that keeps automated services running but stays invisible to their users [-@gray2019].
- **Fauxtomation.** Taylor uses this term for systems that are presented as automated but depend on hidden human work. In her words, it "aims to disguise the real character of the work in question" [-@taylor2018].
- **Feedback work.** Instruction-following models learn from human judgment. For InstructGPT, OpenAI hired about 40 contractors through Upwork and Scale AI to write example answers and to rank model outputs [@ouyang2022].
- **Instructions shape data.** Miceli and Posada studied outsourced data work in Venezuela and Argentina. Instructions, interfaces, and performance metrics reproduce the worldview of the requesters, and precarious conditions make workers obedient to them [@miceli2022].

### 3. Extraction concerns people who never agreed

Training data come from the work of writers, artists, photographers, and translators. Their consent was rarely asked. Crawford describes the collection of data at this scale as a form of extraction, next to the extraction of minerals and labor [-@crawford2021, chs. 2–3]. Copyright, consent, and provenance are therefore questions of labor too.

### 4. Recourse is unevenly distributed

A person who is harmed by an output can often not find out which data, which worker, or which decision caused it. Bender et al. warn that undocumented training data "perpetuates harm without recourse" [@bender2021, 615].

## Evidence and limits

::: {.callout-note title="What the evidence shows"}

- Investigative journalism and interview studies document the conditions of outsourced data work [@perrigo2023; @miceli2022; @gray2019].
- Developers' own papers document that human feedback is part of the training [@ouyang2022].

:::

::: {.callout-caution title="Limits of the evidence"}

- Most contracts between AI companies and suppliers are confidential. Single cases come from leaks, investigations, or interviews.
- Working conditions differ across suppliers, countries, and years. One case does not describe the whole industry.
- The companies dispute some details of the reported cases. The case below states where they do.

:::

## Case: safety labeling for ChatGPT in Kenya {#case-sama}

::: {.callout-note title="Documented case"}
This case comes from an investigation by _TIME_, based on interviews and documents [@perrigo2023].
:::

To make ChatGPT less toxic, OpenAI needed a detector for violent, hateful, and sexual content. The detector needed labeled examples. From late 2021, OpenAI contracted Sama, a San Francisco-based outsourcing firm, to label tens of thousands of text passages in Nairobi, Kenya [@perrigo2023].

| Item            | Reported fact                                                                                                 |
| --------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| Task            | Label text passages that describe violence, hate speech, and sexual abuse                                     |
| Take-home wage  | About USD 1.32 to 2 per hour, by seniority and performance                                                    |
| Workload        | Workers reported 150 to 250 passages per nine-hour shift. Sama said 70.                                       |
| Contracts       | Three contracts worth about USD 200,000. OpenAI said it paid about USD 150,000, because the work ended early. |
| End of the work | Sama ended the work in February 2022, eight months early                                                      |

: Reported facts. Source: Perrigo [-@perrigo2023]. {.striped}

_TIME_ interviewed four Sama employees who worked on the project. All four "described being mentally scarred by the work". They had access to "wellness" counseling, but all four said that the sessions did not help [@perrigo2023]. OpenAI said that it works "hard to build safe and useful AI systems that limit bias and harmful content" [@perrigo2023].

![OpenAI commissions labeling from Sama. Sama manages text labelers in Nairobi. The labels help train a toxicity detector built into ChatGPT. Documented case: Perrigo (2023). Original diagram, CC BY 4.0.](../../assets/cases/03-safety-labor.svg){fig-alt="A chain separates commissioning, supplier management, and human labeling from the resulting text labels, safety detector, and ChatGPT product."}

This case concerns safety labeling. The separate work of writing and ranking model answers for human-feedback training is documented by Ouyang et al. [@ouyang2022].

**Why this case.** The safety of a product for its users depended on work that exposed other people to harm. The users never saw this work. The case asks where the responsibility of a researcher who uses the product begins.

### Worked matrix

::: {.callout-note title="How to complete a focused matrix"}

{{< include _worked-example-03.qmd >}}

:::

The fictional university team is considering ChatGPT. It uses the Kenya investigation as evidence about labeling and contracting [@perrigo2023]. Its judgments about risk and influence are a teaching analysis. Its interventions are **PROPOSED**. The report does not establish every route to complaint or remedy. Write **Unknown from this report** when evidence is missing. Do not infer that no route exists.

## Activity

This Lens has no individual activity. After the four Lens inputs, each participant chooses the Lens that fits their Research Use best. The participants form Lens groups of four, ideally one group for each Lens. The Lens 3 group works for 60 minutes:

1. Each person introduces their Research Use Card.
2. The group applies the four guiding questions below to each Research Use.
3. The group records insights, uncertainties, and disagreements on a flipchart or in a shared document.
4. The group nominates a spokesperson for the plenary.

**Guiding questions for Lens 3**

{{< include _guiding-questions-03.qmd >}}

Write **Unknown** where evidence is missing: an unknown is a finding. Describe the use, not the data. Do not show confidential, personal, or unpublished research data. If a Research Use cannot be discussed openly, use the [Kenya case](#case-sama) instead.

The questions of all four Lenses are on one shared slide of the [course day deck](../slides/06-day.qmd).

## Output

The flipchart or the shared document of the Lens 3 group: insights, uncertainties, and disagreements for each Research Use. In the plenary, the spokesperson reports the conceptual insights, not the individual Research Uses. The [syllabus](../syllabus.qmd#lens-groups) gives the three plenary questions.

## Slides

Open the [Lens 3 slide deck](../slides/03-lifecycle-labor.qmd). Press `S` for the presenter notes.

::: {.callout-note title="For teachers" collapse="true"}
**Timing (15 minutes).** The Kenya case, 5 minutes. The concepts and the worked matrix, 10 minutes. The Lens group applies the four guiding questions later in the morning.

**Prompts.**

- "Which work in your own research is invisible in the final publication?"
- "If an output of this system harms someone, whom can that person contact?"
- "Which stage of the lifecycle does your institution control through procurement or rules?"

**Link to the afternoon.** Keep unknown routes to recourse visible. Panarchy asks at which level someone could investigate or change them. An unknown route is not evidence that no route exists.

**Difficult moments.** Some participants work with outsourced labor themselves, for example through crowdsourcing platforms. Invite them to share practice, not to defend it. Point to fair-pay guidelines of their discipline where they exist.

**Preparation.** Show the completed matrix as the example of this Lens. The slide deck starts with the case. The lesson page keeps its standard section order. Its documentary image comes from Mathenge's worker-led account [@mathenge2024], a separate source from TIME's interviews. It does not show the labeling task. Do not play the film without reviewing its content note.

**Lens group.** Circulate during the group work. If a group gets stuck, ask one guiding question at a time. If a Research Use cannot be discussed openly, offer the case of this Lens.
:::
